newsitem.title: USA: Hearing begins on fatal Delta takeoff accident.
newsitem.headline: Hearing begins on fatal Delta takeoff accident.

text.p: Federal investigators began a hearing Wednesday into the failure of an engine on a Delta Air Lines plane taking off from Pensacola, Florida, last summer that killed a Michigan woman and her son.

The first witness to testify before the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was an official from Volvo Aero Corp. The Swedish company manufactured the titanium fan hub in the left engine which ruptured, sending shrapnel into the fuselage of the MD-88 jet carrying 142 passengers.

Witnesses from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Pratt & Whitney, a unit of United Technologies, and Delta Air Lines were scheduled to appear during the three-day hearing, which was expected to concentrate on technical matters.

"What is of great concern here is the whole manufacturing process and the whole oversight of it and what quality control checks are in place and have they changed," John Goglia, the NTSB member chairing the hearing, told Reuters. "This engine has been in production for 30 years."

Among those in the audience was Randy Sexton, of Scottville, Mich., whose wife and 12-year-old son were killed in the accident which occurred as Delta flight 1288 was gaining speed for takeoff. "A lot of this hasn't sunk in yet," he told Reuters. Two other members of the Sexton family were injured.
Pilots aborted their takeoff before the plane left the ground at Pensacola Regional Airport on July 6, 1996. Three dozen passengers left through emergency exits after the plane came to a stop.

The NTSB concluded that fatigue cracking occurred in a tie-rod hole of the fan hub as a result of manufacturing. After the accident, the FAA ordered removal of fan hubs from six Pratt & Whitney JT8D-200 turbofan engines that were found to have suffered similar cracking.

The FAA has proposed more aggressive inspections to prevent fan hub failure because of tie-rod, counterweight or bushed hold cracking. The inspections include use of a flourescent penetrant inspection developed by Delta Air Lines and an eddy current test which uses an electrical field to detect cracks.
The agency estimates that there are 2,624 engines of the affected design worldwide, including 1,279 engines installed on aircraft registered in the United States.

Goglia, a former airline mechanic, said this type of parts failure was unlikely to reoccur. "It appears that this disc was a stand-alone abnormality, though we have asked for inspections of all similar type discs," he said. "We are going to err on the side of prudence."
